newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Finger-pointing Malaysia has "rogue" market past.
newsitem.headline: Finger-pointing Malaysia has "rogue" market past.

text.p: Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad blames "rogue speculators" for the recent attack on Southeast Asian currencies, exactly the words some in the West had used to describe Malaysia's central Bank Negara not so long ago.
The sharp-tongued Mahathir accused speculators of trying to "destroy all the progress that we have made" in a speech to the Association of South East Asian Nations on Thursday.
But, analysts say, Malaysia does not have too much to complain about.

Bank Negara, an aggressive currency speculator right up to the early 1990s, had a few years ago even ignored warnings from the Bank of England and the U.S. Federal Reserve that its moves were causing instability in the financial markets.
Bank Negara had called it "active reserves management".
Until 1993, when it lost billions of dollars defending the ringgit and speculating in other currencies, Bank Negara was feared for its immense power over the financial markets.
Now, the speculators are doing unto Bank Negara what it once did unto others, the analysts said.
"The market knows that they were big speculators of currencies, mainly G-7 (Group of Seven) currencies. What goes around comes around," said a currency analyst in Singapore.
Having refrained since 1993 from "playing" the market, Malaysia is finding the going tough as speculators sell down the ringgit, unbothered by threats even from Mahathir.
The ringgit has in the last two weeks lost over five percent to around 2.65/dollar and the fall is expected to continue, along with declines in other regional currencies.
The tables have surely turned for the Malaysia of the fabled pre-dawn raids on the London Stock Exchange and the tin market speculation fiasco.

Bank Negara's speculative activities came to an abrupt end in 1992/93 when it made wrong bets on the sterling's direction. It embarrassingly lost $2.2 billion during a European Exchange Rate Mechanism crisis.
"They have stopped speculative plays in the market. How much in losses can one take," said a dealer at a European bank.
But Bank Negara's massive losses were to the gain of a raft of speculators who took opposite positions on sterling, including American financier George Soros.

Interestingly, Mahathir this week blamed a "powerful American financier", whom he has not identified, as one of those behind the plunge of regional currencies, saying there was a political agenda behind the attacks.
Dealers in Singapore and London have named Soros and his Quantum group as one of those leading the attack on Southeast Asian currencies. Soros has denied involvement.
But currency speculation was not Malaysia's only claim to speculative notoriety.

In the early 1980s Malaysia tried to corner the world's tin market, but had to abandon it with huge losses. It hoped to push up tin prices and force traders on the London Metals Exchange (LME) to buy the commodity from Malaysia at higher prices.
But the plan backfired when the LME changed some of its rules while other producers provided fresh supplies and the United States released its huge tin stockpile.
Malaysia's losses were never officially declared, though market estimates then put them as high as $500 million.
But not all its big market plays resulted in losses.
In the 1970s, Malaysia successfully launched a series of spectacular raids on prime British companies with assets in Malaysia, showing it too can profit from open markets.
Malaysia first captured London Tin Corp, then the world's largest tin group, on the London Stock Exchange.
It later bagged large plantation firms Sime Darby Holdings and Guthrie Corp. All the companies have since been turned into conglomerates run by Malaysians.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
